target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reliably remove work-time barriers and help low-income workers vote
objection: A federal holiday does not generally force private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many low-income retail/service workers would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday would not reliably remove the scheduling barrier for the people most affected.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday is worthwhile even if it does not eliminate every barrier because it can be combined with other reforms
objection: Even if a holiday can be paired with other reforms, the holiday itself is still a weaker and less direct policy than state-guaranteed time off to vote or automatic voter registration, which more reliably change access.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would reduce scheduling barriers for many people despite some private employers staying open
objection: If a voter still must work during polling hours and cannot get guaranteed time off, the holiday leaves the key scheduling barrier intact for typical working voters, especially low-income workers.

target: AG1’s reliance on OECD precedent to argue that holiday/weekend elections are feasible and not inherently ineffective
objection: The fact that many OECD countries use weekends or holidays does not show that a U.S. federal holiday will work similarly, because private employers here are not required to close or give paid leave, so the comparison does not answer the practical enforcement problem.

target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a holiday would not leave low-income workers worse off because it would not remove voting options
objection: A holiday can remove voting opportunities by closing school-based polling locations, forcing voters to travel farther or wait longer; low-income voters with limited transportation and flexibility would be hit hardest by that loss of local polling sites.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status would reduce scheduling clashes for low-income retail/service workers by changing business schedules
objection: In many retail and service workplaces, holiday status does not meaningfully reduce staffing needs or required shifts because businesses remain open and staffing is driven by customer demand, so the overlap with voting hours often stays the same.

target: AG1’s claim that reduced work/school overlap is enough to give low-income workers reliable voting time
objection: Low-income workers may still need paid or job-protected leave to make voting time practically usable; without it, they can lose wages or face job consequences, so overlap reduction alone is not reliable access.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably create enough free time for low-income workers to complete voting despite travel and waiting
objection: Voting can require travel plus uncertain waiting and processing time, and a holiday may leave only a limited free window for shift workers, so reduced overlap does not reliably ensure they can finish voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would typically expand many low-income workers’ free window to most of the day
objection: Many low-income hourly workers would still be scheduled during much of Election Day even on a holiday, because private employers are not required to reduce or cancel shifts, so their free window would not usually expand enough.

target: AG1’s claim that reduced scheduling overlap generally gives enough practical time for hourly workers to vote
objection: Even if some work/school obligations are reduced, polling-place voting can still take longer than the remaining free window because of travel and variable waiting times, so the holiday does not reliably translate into completed voting.
